### Geographic Proximity and Distance Instruments {#sec-distance-iv}

Distance is the most heavily used instrument in applied economics, and it is the family a
referee is most likely to have seen before. The reason is practical. Administrative data
almost always record where a person lives and where the relevant facility sits, so the
instrument can be constructed after the fact at no cost, it varies continuously, and it has
an economic interpretation that any reader accepts immediately: travelling further is more
expensive, so people who live further away take up less of whatever the facility supplies.
Section \@ref(sec-workhorse-instruments) lists proximity as one of the workhorse families;
this section develops it, because the arguments that decide whether a distance instrument
survives review are specific enough to be worth stating in full.

#### The Design Logic

Let $D_i$ be the treatment whose effect we want, $Y_i$ the outcome, and $Z_i$ some measure of
how far unit $i$ lives from the facility that supplies $D$. The instrument is supposed to work
through a cost channel. Write take-up as the solution to a decision problem in which the
benefit of treatment is $B_i$ and the cost is $C_i = c(Z_i) + \kappa_i$, with $c(\cdot)$
increasing in distance. Then

$$
D_i = \mathbb{1}\{B_i > c(Z_i) + \kappa_i\},
$$

and distance shifts take-up without, in the ideal case, entering the benefit $B_i$ or the
outcome equation directly. That is the whole identifying claim: distance is a price, and a
price that the analyst did not set.

Three consequences follow, and they organize everything below.

First, the estimand is a local one. Compliers are the units for whom $B_i$ sits inside the
window that distance moves, so the [LATE](#sec-monotonicity-assumption) recovered by a distance
instrument is the effect for people near the margin of take-up on the cost dimension. That
group is rarely the population of policy interest, and it is systematically different from the
always-takers, who would travel any distance.

Second, monotonicity is an assumption about the sign of $c'(\cdot)$ holding for everyone.
It is usually reasonable, since almost nobody is made more likely to attend college by living
further from one, but it fails in settings where distance also proxies for something desirable,
for example when the nearest hospital is the low quality one and distance to the nearest
facility is negatively correlated with distance to a good facility.

Third, and this is where most distance instruments die, location is chosen. The unit decided
where to live, or its parents did, and the facility's operator decided where to build. Neither
decision is random, and both are plausibly correlated with the outcome. The exclusion
restriction for a distance instrument is therefore almost never an argument about geography.
It is an argument about residential sorting and facility siting.

#### Where the Family Appears

| Setting | Distance measure | Instruments for | Representative study |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Returns to schooling | Grew up near a four-year college | Years of education | @card2001estimating |
| Intergenerational human capital | College openings in the county at age 17 | Mother's education | @currie2003mother |
| Comparative effectiveness in medicine | Differential distance to a hospital with catheterization capability | Intensive cardiac treatment | @mcclellan1994does |
| Neonatal care | Excess travel time to a high-level neonatal intensive care unit | Delivery at a high-level unit | @baiocchi2010building |
| School competition | Number of streams and rivers bounding potential districts | Degree of Tiebout choice | @hoxby2000does, disputed by @rothstein2007does |
| Internal capital allocation | Travel time from headquarters to plant, shifted by new airline routes | Managerial proximity | @giroud2013proximity |

Table: (\#tab:distiv-applications) Distance and proximity instruments across literatures. The measure differs, but the identifying claim is always that distance prices take-up without entering the outcome equation.

Two patterns are worth naming. The first is that the credible members of this family rarely use
raw distance. They use a difference of distances, or a change in distance produced by an event,
precisely because the level of distance is the part that is chosen. The second is that the
family has a long history of contested applications: @rothstein2007does could not reproduce the
key result of @hoxby2000does once the stream-counting instrument was reconstructed, which is a
reminder that a distance instrument is only as good as the measurement behind it.

#### Replication: College Proximity and the Return to Schooling

The canonical application instruments years of schooling with an indicator for having grown up
near a four-year college. The design and the data come from Card's work on the returns to
schooling, developed at length in @card2001estimating, using the National Longitudinal Survey
of Young Men. The data ship with the `ivreg` package, so the entire exercise is reproducible.

```{r distiv-data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ivreg)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(modelsummary)

data("SchoolingReturns", package = "ivreg")

card <- within(SchoolingReturns, {
  lwage  <- log(wage)
  # "near a four-year college" pools the public and private categories
  near4  <- as.integer(nearcollege4 != "none")
  near2  <- as.integer(nearcollege2 == "yes")
  black  <- as.integer(ethnicity == "afam")
  southD <- as.integer(south == "yes")
  smsaD  <- as.integer(smsa  == "yes")
  lib14  <- as.integer(library14 == "yes")
})

c(n = nrow(card), share_near_4yr = round(mean(card$near4), 3))
```

The controls are the standard human-capital set: a quadratic in potential experience, plus
indicators for race, southern residence, and metropolitan residence. We fit ordinary least
squares, the first stage, the reduced form, and two-stage least squares, and then a
specification that adds parental education and household structure at age fourteen.

```{r distiv-main, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
base <- "experience + I(experience^2) + black + southD + smsaD"
fam  <- paste(base, "+ feducation + meducation + fameducation + parents14")
f    <- function(s) as.formula(s)

ols   <- lm(f(paste("lwage ~ education +", base)), data = card)
first <- lm(f(paste("education ~ near4 +", base)), data = card)
rform <- lm(f(paste("lwage ~ near4 +", base)),     data = card)
iv    <- ivreg(f(paste("lwage ~ education +", base, "| near4 +", base)), data = card)
ivfam <- ivreg(f(paste("lwage ~ education +", fam,  "| near4 +", fam)),  data = card)

HC <- function(m) vcovHC(m, type = "HC1")

modelsummary(
  list("OLS" = ols, "First stage" = first, "Reduced form" = rform,
       "IV" = iv, "IV + background" = ivfam),
  vcov = HC,
  stars = TRUE,
  gof_omit = "IC|Log|Adj|RMSE|F$",
  coef_map = c(education = "Years of education",
               near4     = "Grew up near 4-year college"),
  output = "kableExtra",
  title = paste(
    "College proximity as an instrument for schooling in the National",
    "Longitudinal Survey of Young Men. The first-stage and reduced-form",
    "columns report the two regressions whose ratio is the just-identified",
    "IV estimate in the fourth column. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity",
    "robust."
  )
)
```

```{r distiv-strength, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fs_F <- waldtest(first, "near4", vcov = HC(first))$F[2]
c(first_stage_coef = round(coef(first)["near4"], 4),
  first_stage_F    = round(fs_F, 2),
  reduced_form     = round(coef(rform)["near4"], 4),
  ratio_RF_over_FS = round(coef(rform)["near4"] / coef(first)["near4"], 4),
  iv_coef          = round(coef(iv)["education"], 4))
```

Three things in this output deserve comment.

The first stage is real but modest. Growing up near a four-year college raises completed
schooling by about a third of a year, with a robust first-stage $F$ around 17.5. That clears
the conventional rule of thumb of 10 but sits well below the thresholds that
Section \@ref(sec-tf-procedure) shows are needed before the usual $t$-based confidence interval
can be read at face value.

The ratio of the reduced form to the first stage reproduces the IV coefficient exactly, which
is the arithmetic of the just-identified Wald estimator and a useful check that the controls
enter both stages identically.

The IV estimate is roughly `r round(coef(iv)["education"] / coef(ols)["education"], 1)` times
the OLS estimate, about 13 log points per year of schooling against 7.4. This is the opposite of
what the textbook ability-bias story predicts. If OLS were contaminated by unobserved ability
that raises both schooling and wages, instrumenting should push the estimate down, not up.
@card2001estimating treats this pattern, which recurs across the schooling IV literature, as
evidence for heterogeneous returns: proximity moves the schooling of people from
lower-education backgrounds, whose marginal return is above the population average, so the
LATE legitimately exceeds the average treatment effect. @kling2001interpreting makes the same
point formally, showing which subpopulation each schooling instrument recovers.
@cameron2004estimation tests the borrowing-constraint interpretation that would rationalize
those high marginal returns and finds little support for it, which leaves the gap between OLS
and IV as a genuinely open question rather than a settled story. The alternative reading, that
the gap reflects a violation of the exclusion restriction rather than heterogeneity, is exactly
what the next subsection quantifies.

#### Show and Tell: Weak-Instrument Inference, Sorting, and Sensitivity

A distance instrument with an $F$ of 17.5 is strong enough to escape the worst weak-instrument
pathologies but not strong enough for the Wald confidence interval to be trusted without a
check. Section \@ref(sec-anderson-rubin-approach) gives the remedy. Because the model is just
identified with a single instrument, the Anderson-Rubin confidence set can be built directly by
grid inversion: for each candidate $\beta_0$, subtract $\beta_0 \cdot \text{education}$ from the
outcome and test whether the instrument still predicts the residual.

```{r distiv-ar, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ar_pvalue <- function(b0) {
  card$yadj <- card$lwage - b0 * card$education
  m <- lm(f(paste("yadj ~ near4 +", base)), data = card)
  waldtest(m, "near4", vcov = HC(m))[["Pr(>F)"]][2]
}

grid    <- seq(-0.10, 0.60, by = 0.001)
ar_keep <- grid[vapply(grid, ar_pvalue, numeric(1)) > 0.05]
wald_ci <- coefci(iv, "education", vcov. = HC(iv))

rbind(Wald = round(as.numeric(wald_ci), 3),
      AR   = round(c(min(ar_keep), max(ar_keep)), 3))
```

The Anderson-Rubin interval is shifted right and noticeably asymmetric relative to the Wald
interval. Both exclude zero here, so the qualitative conclusion survives, but the upper end of
the weak-instrument-robust set reaches returns that the Wald interval rules out. Reporting only
the Wald interval would understate how much the data still permit.

Now the exclusion restriction. The objection to college proximity is that families who live
near colleges differ from families who do not, so proximity may raise wages through channels
other than schooling. That objection is testable in one direction: we can at least ask whether
proximity is correlated with observable background.

```{r distiv-sorting, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
sorting <- lm(near4 ~ feducation + meducation + lib14 + black + southD + smsaD,
              data = card)
round(coeftest(sorting, vcov = HC(sorting))[, c(1, 2, 4)], 4)
```

It is. Growing up near a four-year college is strongly associated with living in a metropolitan
area, with not living in the South, with having a library card at fourteen, and with father's
education. None of that proves the exclusion restriction fails, since the specification controls
for metropolitan and southern residence directly. But it does establish that proximity is a
marker of advantaged origins, which is precisely the mechanism through which a direct effect on
wages would operate.

The productive response is not another balance table but a sensitivity analysis in the style of
Section \@ref(sec-plausibly-exogenous). Suppose the instrument enters the outcome equation
directly with coefficient $\gamma$:

$$
Y_i = \beta\, D_i + \gamma\, Z_i + X_i'\delta + \varepsilon_i .
$$

In a just-identified design the implied estimate is
$\beta(\gamma) = (\pi_{\text{RF}} - \gamma)/\pi_{\text{FS}}$, so the entire result rests on how
much of the reduced form we are willing to attribute to a non-schooling channel.

```{r distiv-sensitivity, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
pi_fs <- coef(first)["near4"]
pi_rf <- coef(rform)["near4"]

union_ci <- function(delta, n = 121) {
  gs <- seq(-delta, delta, length.out = n)
  bounds <- vapply(gs, function(g) {
    card$yadj <- card$lwage - g * card$near4
    m <- ivreg(f(paste("yadj ~ education +", base, "| near4 +", base)), data = card)
    as.numeric(coefci(m, "education", vcov. = HC(m)))
  }, numeric(2))
  c(lower = min(bounds[1, ]), upper = max(bounds[2, ]))
}

cat(sprintf("breakdown gamma (drives beta to zero) = %.4f\n", pi_rf))
for (d in c(0.000, 0.005, 0.010, 0.020)) {
  u <- union_ci(d)
  cat(sprintf("delta = %.3f   union CI = [%6.3f, %6.3f]\n", d, u[1], u[2]))
}
```

This is the number to carry away from the section. The reduced-form effect of proximity on log
wages is 4.5 log points in total. A direct effect of proximity on wages of that size, arising
through any channel other than schooling, drives the estimated return to zero. And the union of
confidence intervals already contains zero once we allow a direct effect of only two log points,
under half the reduced form. Given what the sorting regression showed about who lives near
colleges, a two log point direct effect is not an extravagant hypothesis. The design is
informative, but it is fragile in a way that the first-stage $F$ statistic does not reveal.

Finally, proximity to a two-year college provides a second instrument, which makes the model
overidentified and licenses a Hansen $J$ test.

```{r distiv-overid, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ivboth <- ivreg(f(paste("lwage ~ education +", base, "| near4 + near2 +", base)),
                data = card)
summary(ivboth, diagnostics = TRUE)$diagnostics
```

The $J$ statistic does not reject at conventional levels. As the discussion of overidentification
tests earlier in this chapter stresses, and as Section \@ref(sec-instruments-disagree) develops,
that is consistent with both instruments being valid and also consistent with both being invalid
in the same direction, which is exactly the scenario a sorting story predicts, since two-year and
four-year college proximity are driven by the same urban geography.

#### Differential Distance: the Design Fix

The strongest members of this family do not use distance to the facility. They use the
difference between the distance to a facility of the relevant type and the distance to the
nearest facility of any type. @mcclellan1994does introduced this construction for the effect of
intensive cardiac treatment on mortality among elderly heart attack patients, instrumenting
catheterization with the extra distance a patient would have to travel to reach a hospital that
offers it, relative to the nearest hospital.

The logic of the fix is worth stating precisely. Raw distance to a catheterization hospital is
confounded because it is essentially distance to a city, and city residents differ from rural
residents in health, income, and much else. Differential distance nets out that common component.
Two patients who both live twenty miles from their nearest hospital, one of which happens to offer
catheterization and one of which does not, are far more comparable than two patients at different
distances from a catheterization hospital. The instrument now varies with the composition of
nearby facilities rather than with the patient's position in the urban hierarchy. The finding was
that the mortality benefit of intensive treatment was far smaller than the observational
comparison suggested, which is the payoff of taking the design seriously.

@baiocchi2010building push the construction further by combining differential distance with
matching. Their near-far design pairs units that are similar on covariates but far apart on the
instrument, which strengthens the first stage within the matched sample and sharpens the
comparison. This is the practical answer to the weak-instrument problem in this family: rather
than accept a diluted instrument over the full sample, build a subsample in which the instrument
does real work. It also connects the family directly to
[matching](#sec-matching-methods), which is otherwise treated as the alternative to IV rather
than as a complement to it.

The general lesson transfers. Whenever raw distance is confounded by a location gradient, look
for a differenced or event-driven version:

-   differential distance, as in @mcclellan1994does;
-   a change in distance, as when @giroud2013proximity uses the introduction of new airline routes
    to generate within-pair reductions in headquarters-to-plant travel time, holding the pair fixed;
-   a change in the set of nearby facilities, as when @currie2003mother uses college openings in a
    county, which shifts proximity for successive cohorts in the same place.

Each of these converts a level, which is chosen, into a difference or a change, which is easier to
argue was not.

#### Application in Business and Finance

The business-school version of this design is @giroud2013proximity, which asks whether the
physical distance between a firm's headquarters and its plants affects how capital is allocated
inside the firm. Raw distance is hopeless as an instrument here, since firms choose plant
locations for reasons correlated with plant prospects. The design instead uses the opening of new
airline routes that indirectly reduce travel time between an existing headquarters and an existing
plant, comparing the same pair before and after, against pairs unaffected by the route change.
Proximity increases plant-level investment and productivity.

The same construction is available in a range of applied settings. Distance to the nearest branch
instruments for banking relationships; distance to a distribution center instruments for delivery
speed; drive time to a store instruments for channel choice. In each case the referee's question
is the same, and the answer that works is the same: show that you are using a change in distance
or a difference of distances rather than the level, and show what the sorting regression looks
like.

For expert-witness and policy work, the sensitivity calculation above is the deliverable, not the
point estimate. An opposing expert will not attack the first stage, which is visible and strong.
They will argue that proximity captures the local economy. The right preparation is to state, in
advance, how large a direct effect would have to be to overturn the conclusion, and to place that
magnitude against evidence on what proximity is worth through other channels.

#### Checklist

Before relying on a distance instrument:

1.  State the cost channel explicitly. If distance does not plausibly enter the take-up cost, it
    is not an instrument, it is a proxy for geography.
2.  Prefer a difference or a change to a level. Differential distance, distance changes from
    infrastructure events, and facility openings are all more defensible than raw distance.
3.  Run the sorting regression and report it. Who lives near the facility is the substance of the
    exclusion argument.
4.  Report weak-instrument-robust inference. Distance instruments routinely land in the range
    where the Wald interval is optimistic.
5.  Report a breakdown value of $\gamma$, not just a point estimate. In a just-identified design
    the whole reduced form is the budget, and a violation worth a fraction of it is usually enough
    to overturn the result.
6.  Characterize the compliers. The people whose behavior distance moves are a specific and
    usually disadvantaged group, and the estimand is their effect, not the population's.
7.  Remember @rosenzweig2000natural. A natural experiment does not interpret itself; the economic
    model determines what the instrument identifies, and distance instruments are unusually prone
    to being read as though they answered a more general question than they do.
